rooms.about: A year of reading great stories, poems and plays from around the world, from ancient epics to modern novels, while sharpening analytical and argumentative writing.

learn: World literature means works written in many languages and places, often read in translation. Reading them lets us see how people in different times and cultures answer the same big questions about love, power, death and justice.

Context matters. Before reading, ask when and where the work was written, who its first audience was and what beliefs were common then. Context does not excuse everything in a text, but it helps you understand the choices an author made.

Translation is an act of interpretation. A translator must choose between matching the exact words and capturing the tone, rhythm or humor. Comparing two translations of the same line can reveal how much meaning lives in word choice.
A strong reader keeps two lenses open: what the text meant in its own setting, and what it means to readers today. Good literary essays move carefully between both.
units.try: Find two different English translations of the opening lines of any famous poem or epic (your library or school anthology will have several). Write down three words that differ between them, and for each, explain in one sentence how the change shifts the mood or meaning.
check: Why does reading context help with a work of world literature?
It explains the beliefs and situation the author wrote within
It tells you the work is always correct
It replaces the need to read the text
What is one challenge a translator faces?
Choosing between exact wording and capturing tone
Changing the plot to fit modern readers

units.t: Ancient Epics: Gilgamesh and the Hero
learn: An epic is a long narrative poem about a heroic figure whose deeds matter to a whole people. The Epic of Gilgamesh, from ancient Mesopotamia and written on clay tablets more than 3,500 years ago, is one of the oldest surviving works of literature.

Gilgamesh begins as a proud king who abuses his power. His friendship with Enkidu changes him, and Enkidu’s death sends him on a quest for immortality. He fails, but he returns home wiser, accepting that human achievements, like the walls of his city, are what endure.

Epics share common features: an invocation or formal opening, a hero of great strength, supernatural beings, long journeys, and repeated phrases called epithets that helped storytellers remember the poem.
The hero’s journey is a pattern many stories follow: a call to adventure, trials, a low point, a transformation and a return. Recognizing it helps you compare stories across cultures.
units.try: Pick a modern movie or novel you know well. Map it onto the hero’s journey with five labeled stages: call, trials, lowest point, transformation, return. Then write one paragraph comparing how its hero changes with how Gilgamesh changes.
check: That human life is limited and lasting deeds matter
What is an epithet in an epic?
A repeated descriptive phrase attached to a name
The final chapter of the poem

learn: Tragedy began in ancient Athens in the 400s BCE as plays performed at religious festivals. A tragedy shows a person of high standing who falls into disaster, often because of a flaw or error in judgment, called hamartia.

In Sophocles’ Oedipus Rex, Oedipus tries to escape a prophecy and in doing so fulfills it. Dramatic irony is strong here: the audience knows the truth long before Oedipus does, which makes every confident line he speaks painful to hear.
Greek plays used a chorus, a group that sang and commented on the action and often spoke for the community. Violence usually happened offstage and was reported by a messenger.
The philosopher Aristotle wrote that tragedy creates pity and fear in the audience and then releases them, a process he called catharsis.
units.try: Read a short scene from a Greek tragedy in your anthology. List two moments of dramatic irony: what does the audience know that the character does not? Then write three sentences on how that gap makes the scene more powerful.
check: A tragic hero’s flaw or error in judgment
The audience knows something a character does not
The play ends in a wedding

learn: A literary analysis essay makes an arguable claim about how a text works and proves it with evidence. A claim like “The author uses darkness to show guilt” can be argued; a summary like “The story is about a crime” cannot.

Body paragraphs follow a pattern: a topic sentence that supports the thesis, a short quotation or detail, and analysis that explains how the evidence proves the point. Analysis should be longer than the quote.
Integrate quotations smoothly. Introduce them with your own words, keep them short, and cite the page or line. Never drop a quote into a paragraph alone.
A good conclusion does more than repeat. It explains why the insight matters, for example what it reveals about the culture or about human nature.
units.try: Write a thesis about a story you read this year that answers a how or why question. Then write one body paragraph: topic sentence, a quotation of no more than 15 words, and at least three sentences of analysis explaining specific word choices.
check: Which of these is an arguable thesis?
The repeated storms show the hero’s inner chaos
In a body paragraph, what should be longer than the quotation?

units.t: Shakespeare’s World: Julius Caesar or Macbeth
learn: William Shakespeare (1564–1616) wrote about 37 plays in English verse. Many tenth graders study a tragedy such as Julius Caesar or Macbeth, both about ambition, power and the cost of violence.

Shakespeare often used blank verse: unrhymed lines of iambic pentameter, ten syllables in a pattern of unstressed then stressed, as in “so FOUL and FAIR a DAY i HAVE not SEEN.” Common characters often speak in prose instead.
A soliloquy is a speech a character gives alone on stage, revealing private thoughts. An aside is a short comment to the audience that other characters do not hear.
Rhetoric matters in Julius Caesar. Brutus appeals to reason and honor, while Mark Antony uses emotion, repetition and irony (“Brutus is an honorable man”) to turn the crowd.
units.try: Choose a soliloquy of about 10–15 lines. Rewrite it line by line in modern everyday English. Then mark the stressed syllables in two original lines to hear the iambic rhythm out loud.
check: A speech a character gives alone revealing thoughts
A song sung by the chorus
How many syllables are in a line of iambic pentameter?

learn: Rhetoric is the art of persuasion. Aristotle described three appeals: ethos (credibility of the speaker), pathos (emotion of the audience) and logos (logic and evidence). Strong arguments usually blend all three.
A complete argument includes a claim, reasons, evidence, a counterclaim and a rebuttal. Addressing the other side fairly makes your position stronger, not weaker.

Watch for logical fallacies: an ad hominem attacks the person instead of the idea; a straw man misrepresents the other view; a false dilemma pretends only two choices exist; a hasty generalization draws a conclusion from too few examples.
Famous speeches from world history, such as those by Nelson Mandela at his 1964 trial, are rich models for studying how speakers combine appeals.
units.try: Pick a debatable school issue, such as later start times. Write a five-sentence argument with a claim, two reasons with evidence, one counterclaim, and a rebuttal. Label each sentence with ethos, pathos or logos.
check: Which appeal relies on facts and reasoning?
Saying “You can’t trust her idea, she’s always late” is which fallacy?

units.t: Things Fall Apart and Postcolonial Literature
learn: Chinua Achebe’s Things Fall Apart (1958) tells the story of Okonkwo, a respected Igbo man in Nigeria, whose life and village are shaken by the arrival of British missionaries and colonial government in the late 1800s.

Achebe wrote partly to answer European novels that showed Africans as people without history. He presents Igbo society as complex, with laws, religion, art, debate and its own flaws, before colonization disrupts it.
Postcolonial literature is writing from or about countries that were once colonies. It often explores identity, language, cultural loss and the effects of power.
Okonkwo’s fear of seeming weak drives many of his choices. Readers can analyze how personal flaws and historical forces combine to cause tragedy.
units.try: Make a two-column chart: Igbo life before the missionaries and changes after their arrival. Add at least four details to each column, then write a paragraph explaining which change you think the novel presents as most important and why.
check: Where is Things Fall Apart set?
What is one aim Achebe had in writing the novel?
To show African society as complex with its own history

learn: Poetry compresses meaning into careful sound and image. Key tools include imagery (sensory detail), metaphor and simile (comparisons), personification, and symbolism.

Forms travel across cultures. The Japanese haiku uses three lines, traditionally 5, 7 and 5 syllables, often with a seasonal image. The Persian ghazal uses linked couplets that repeat an ending word. The sonnet has 14 lines.
Sound devices include alliteration (repeated first sounds), assonance (repeated vowel sounds), rhyme and meter. Free verse drops regular meter but still uses rhythm and line breaks for effect.
To analyze a poem, read it aloud twice, identify the speaker and situation, mark shifts in tone, and ask how the form supports the meaning.
units.try: Write a haiku about something you saw today with 5, 7 and 5 syllables. Then write two lines of free verse about the same thing, and explain in two sentences how the different forms change the feel.
check: How many lines does a sonnet have?
A poem of linked couplets that repeat an ending word

units.t: Modern World Novels and Narrative Technique
learn: Modern novelists experiment with how stories are told. Point of view can be first person (“I”), third person limited (one character’s mind) or third person omniscient (many minds).
An unreliable narrator is one whose account we cannot fully trust, because of bias, youth, madness or self-deception. Readers must look past what the narrator says to what the details show.

Magical realism, linked with writers such as Gabriel García Márquez of Colombia, blends ordinary everyday life with calmly described impossible events. The magic often carries political or emotional meaning.
Other techniques include flashback, stream of consciousness (a flow of thoughts) and frame stories, where one story is told inside another.
units.try: Rewrite a short scene from a story you know from a different point of view, about 150 words. Then list two things the reader learns in your version that the original hid, and one thing your version hides.
check: A narrator whose account cannot be fully trusted
A narrator who speaks in third person
A narrator who is a hero
Magical realism mixes everyday life with what?

learn: A research paper answers a focused question using credible sources. Start with a narrow question, such as “How did censorship shape Soviet novels?” rather than “Russian literature.”
Judge sources by authority, accuracy, date and purpose. Scholarly books, academic journals and reputable publishers are strong; anonymous pages are weak.

Take notes in your own words and record citation details. Paraphrase changes both wording and sentence structure; a quote copies exact words in quotation marks. Both must be cited. Using others’ ideas without credit is plagiarism.
MLA style, common in English classes, uses in-text citations like (Achebe 45) and a Works Cited list in alphabetical order at the end.
units.try: Write a research question about a world author you read this year. Then find one print or library source and write a correct MLA Works Cited entry for it, plus one paraphrase and one short quotation with in-text citations.
check: What does MLA in-text citation usually include?
Author’s last name and page number
Using someone’s ideas without credit is called what?

rooms.about: A full year of geometry: reasoning and proof, angles and parallel lines, triangles and congruence, similarity, right triangles and trigonometry, polygons, circles, area, volume and coordinate geometry.

learn: Geometry starts with undefined terms: a point (a location), a line (extends forever both ways) and a plane (a flat surface extending forever). A segment has two endpoints; a ray has one endpoint and goes on forever.
A conditional statement has the form “if p, then q.” Its converse is “if q, then p,” and it may not be true. If both are true, we write a biconditional: “p if and only if q.”

Inductive reasoning finds patterns from examples and makes a conjecture. Deductive reasoning uses definitions, postulates and proven theorems to reach a certain conclusion. Proofs use deductive reasoning.
The midpoint of a segment from (x₁, y₁) to (x₂, y₂) is ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2). The distance is √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²).
units.try:
Find the midpoint and length of the segment from A(1, 2) to B(7, 10).
Step 1: Midpoint = ((1+7)/2, (2+10)/2) = (4, 6).
Step 2: Differences: 7−1 = 6 and 10−2 = 8.
Step 3: Distance = √(6² + 8²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10.
Now try: A(−2, 3) and B(4, 11). (Answer: midpoint (1, 7), length 10.)
check: What is the converse of “If it rains, the ground is wet”?
If the ground is wet, it rains
If it does not rain, the ground is dry
What is the distance from (0, 0) to (3, 4)?

learn: Angles are measured in degrees. Acute is less than 90°, right is 90°, obtuse is between 90° and 180°, straight is 180°. Complementary angles sum to 90°; supplementary angles sum to 180°.
Vertical angles, formed by two crossing lines, are always congruent. A linear pair of angles is supplementary.

When a transversal crosses two parallel lines, corresponding angles are congruent, alternate interior angles are congruent, alternate exterior angles are congruent, and same-side interior angles are supplementary.
The converses are also true, so if corresponding angles are congruent, the lines are parallel. Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is −1.
units.try:
Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One same-side interior angle is (3x + 10)° and the other is (2x + 20)°.
Step 1: Same-side interior angles are supplementary: 3x + 10 + 2x + 20 = 180.
Step 2: 5x + 30 = 180, so 5x = 150 and x = 30.
Step 3: The angles are 100° and 80°. Check: 100 + 80 = 180.
check: Alternate interior angles formed by parallel lines are what?
A line has slope 2. What is the slope of a perpendicular line?

learn: A transformation moves or changes a figure. Rigid motions keep size and shape: translations (slides), reflections (flips) and rotations (turns). Dilations change size but keep shape.
A translation by (a, b) maps (x, y) to (x+a, y+b). Reflecting over the x-axis maps (x, y) to (x, −y); over the y-axis to (−x, y); over y = x to (y, x).
Rotating 90° counterclockwise about the origin maps (x, y) to (−y, x); 180° maps to (−x, −y).
A dilation with center at the origin and scale factor k maps (x, y) to (kx, ky). If k > 1 it enlarges; if 0 < k < 1 it shrinks.
units.try:
Triangle with vertices (1, 2), (3, 2), (1, 5) is rotated 90° counterclockwise about the origin.
Step 1: Use (x, y) → (−y, x).
Step 2: (1, 2) → (−2, 1); (3, 2) → (−2, 3); (1, 5) → (−5, 1).
Now reflect the original over the y-axis. (Answer: (−1, 2), (−3, 2), (−1, 5).)
check: Which transformation is NOT a rigid motion?
Reflecting (4, −3) over the x-axis gives what?

learn: Congruent figures have the same size and shape. Triangles can be proven congruent with SSS (three sides), SAS (two sides and the included angle), ASA, AAS, and for right triangles HL (hypotenuse and leg).
SSA and AAA do NOT prove congruence. AAA only shows the triangles have the same shape.
After proving triangles congruent, use CPCTC: corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent.
A two-column proof lists statements on the left and reasons on the right. Reasons are givens, definitions, postulates or theorems.
units.try:
Given: M is the midpoint of AB and of CD. Prove triangle AMC ≅ triangle BMD.
1. M is the midpoint of AB and CD (Given).
2. AM ≅ BM and CM ≅ DM (Definition of midpoint).
3. Angle AMC ≅ angle BMD (Vertical angles are congruent).
4. Triangle AMC ≅ triangle BMD (SAS).
check: Which is NOT a valid triangle congruence shortcut?
Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent

learn: The angles of any triangle add to 180°. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.
In an isosceles triangle, the base angles opposite the equal sides are congruent. An equilateral triangle has three 60° angles.
Triangle Inequality: the sum of any two sides must be greater than the third. Sides 3, 4 and 8 cannot make a triangle because 3 + 4 < 8.

Special segments: medians meet at the centroid, which is ⅔ of the way from each vertex to the opposite midpoint. Perpendicular bisectors meet at the circumcenter; angle bisectors meet at the incenter; altitudes meet at the orthocenter.
units.try:
An exterior angle of a triangle measures 130°. One remote interior angle is 55°. Find the other.
Step 1: Exterior angle = sum of remote interior angles.
Step 2: 130 = 55 + x, so x = 75°.
Step 3: The third interior angle is 180 − 130 = 50°. Check: 55 + 75 + 50 = 180.
check: Can sides 5, 6 and 12 form a triangle?
Where do the medians of a triangle meet?

learn: Similar figures have the same shape: corresponding angles are congruent and corresponding sides are proportional. The ratio of sides is the scale factor.
Triangles are similar by AA (two pairs of congruent angles), SSS similarity (all sides proportional) or SAS similarity (two sides proportional with equal included angles).
The Triangle Proportionality Theorem: a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally.
If the scale factor is k, the ratio of perimeters is k, the ratio of areas is k², and the ratio of volumes is k³.
units.try:
A 6 ft person casts a 4 ft shadow. At the same time, a tree casts a 30 ft shadow. How tall is the tree?
Step 1: The sun’s angle makes similar triangles (AA).
Step 2: 6/4 = h/30.
Step 3: 4h = 180, so h = 45 ft.
check: Two similar figures have scale factor 3. What is the ratio of their areas?
Which shortcut proves triangles similar using only angles?

learn: The Pythagorean Theorem says a² + b² = c² in a right triangle, with c the hypotenuse. Common triples are 3-4-5, 5-12-13 and 8-15-17.
Special right triangles: in a 45-45-90 triangle the sides are x, x, x√2. In a 30-60-90 triangle the sides are x, x√3, 2x.
Trig ratios for an acute angle: sine = opposite/hypotenuse, cosine = adjacent/hypotenuse, tangent = opposite/adjacent. Remember SOH-CAH-TOA.
Inverse trig functions find angles: if tan A = 0.75, then A = tan⁻¹(0.75) ≈ 36.9°.
units.try:
A ladder 10 m long leans against a wall making a 70° angle with the ground. How high up the wall does it reach?
Step 1: Height is opposite the 70° angle; ladder is the hypotenuse.
Step 2: sin 70° = h/10.
Step 3: h = 10 × sin 70° ≈ 10 × 0.940 = 9.4 m.
check: What is cosine of an angle in a right triangle?
In a 30-60-90 triangle with short leg 5, what is the hypotenuse?

learn: The interior angles of a polygon with n sides add to (n − 2) × 180°. The exterior angles of any convex polygon add to 360°.
A parallelogram has opposite sides parallel and congruent, opposite angles congruent, and diagonals that bisect each other.
A rectangle is a parallelogram with four right angles and congruent diagonals. A rhombus has four congruent sides and perpendicular diagonals. A square is both.
A trapezoid has exactly one pair of parallel sides (in most US textbooks). Its midsegment equals the average of the two bases.
units.try:
Find each interior angle of a regular hexagon.
Step 1: Sum = (6 − 2) × 180 = 720°.
Step 2: Each angle = 720 ÷ 6 = 120°.
Step 3: Check with exterior angles: 360 ÷ 6 = 60°, and 180 − 60 = 120°.
Now try a regular octagon. (Answer: 135°.)
check: What is the sum of interior angles of a pentagon?
Which quadrilateral always has perpendicular diagonals?

learn: A circle is all points a fixed distance (the radius) from a center. Circumference C = 2πr and area A = πr².

A central angle has its vertex at the center and equals its intercepted arc. An inscribed angle has its vertex on the circle and equals half its intercepted arc. An angle inscribed in a semicircle is 90°.
A tangent line touches the circle at one point and is perpendicular to the radius there. Arc length = (θ/360) × 2πr, and sector area = (θ/360) × πr².
The equation of a circle with center (h, k) and radius r is (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r².
units.try:
Find the arc length and sector area for a 60° sector of a circle with radius 9 cm.
Step 1: Fraction of circle = 60/360 = 1/6.
Step 2: Arc length = (1/6) × 2π × 9 = 3π ≈ 9.42 cm.
Step 3: Sector area = (1/6) × π × 81 = 13.5π ≈ 42.4 cm².
check: An inscribed angle intercepts an arc of 80°. What is the angle?

learn: Area formulas: rectangle A = lw, triangle A = ½bh, parallelogram A = bh, trapezoid A = ½(b₁ + b₂)h.
Volume of a prism or cylinder is V = Bh, where B is the area of the base. A cylinder has V = πr²h.
Pyramids and cones hold one third of the matching prism or cylinder: V = ⅓Bh, so a cone has V = ⅓πr²h. A sphere has V = (4/3)πr³ and surface area 4πr².
Cavalieri’s Principle: solids with equal heights and equal cross-section areas at every level have equal volumes.
units.try:
A cone-shaped cup has radius 3 cm and height 8 cm. Find its volume.
Step 1: V = ⅓πr²h.
Step 2: V = ⅓ × π × 9 × 8 = 24π.
Step 3: 24π ≈ 75.4 cm³.
Compare: a cylinder with the same size holds 72π ≈ 226 cm³, three times as much.
check: What is the volume of a sphere with radius 3?
A cone holds what fraction of a cylinder with the same base and height?

rooms.about: An introduction to chemistry: matter and measurement, atomic structure, the periodic table, bonding, reactions, the mole, stoichiometry, gases, solutions, and acids and bases.

learn: Chemistry is the study of matter and how it changes. Matter is anything with mass and volume. A pure substance is either an element (one kind of atom) or a compound (atoms of different elements chemically joined). Mixtures can be homogeneous (uniform, like salt water) or heterogeneous (like sand in water).
Physical changes alter form but not identity, such as melting ice. Chemical changes make new substances, shown by signs like gas bubbles, color change, light, heat or a precipitate.
Scientists use SI units: meter (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), kelvin (temperature) and mole (amount). Prefixes include kilo- (1,000), centi- (1/100) and milli- (1/1,000).
Significant figures show the precision of a measurement. Accuracy means closeness to the true value; precision means closeness of repeated measurements to each other.
units.try:
Convert 2.5 kilometers to centimeters using dimensional analysis.
Step 1: 2.5 km × (1,000 m / 1 km) = 2,500 m.
Step 2: 2,500 m × (100 cm / 1 m) = 250,000 cm.
Step 3: Units cancel diagonally, leaving cm. Answer: 2.5 × 10⁵ cm.
check: How many milligrams are in 1 gram?

learn: Atoms contain protons (positive, in the nucleus), neutrons (neutral, in the nucleus) and electrons (negative, outside the nucleus). Protons and neutrons each have a mass of about 1 atomic mass unit; electrons are about 1/1,836 as heavy.

The atomic number is the number of protons and defines the element. The mass number is protons plus neutrons. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, such as carbon-12 and carbon-14.

Models changed over time: Dalton’s solid spheres, Thomson’s plum pudding with electrons, Rutherford’s gold foil experiment showing a tiny dense nucleus, Bohr’s energy levels, and today’s quantum model of electron clouds.
Electrons occupy energy levels and orbitals (s, p, d, f). An electron configuration like 1s² 2s² 2p⁴ describes oxygen’s 8 electrons.
units.try:
An atom of chlorine-37 has atomic number 17. Find its particles.
Step 1: Protons = atomic number = 17.
Step 2: Neutrons = mass number − protons = 37 − 17 = 20.
Step 3: A neutral atom has electrons = protons = 17.
Now try sodium-23 (atomic number 11). (Answer: 11 p, 12 n, 11 e.)
check: What determines which element an atom is?
What did Rutherford’s gold foil experiment show?
Atoms have a small dense nucleus

learn: The periodic table arranges elements by increasing atomic number. Dmitri Mendeleev published an early version in 1869 and left gaps for elements not yet discovered.

Columns are groups; elements in a group have the same number of valence electrons and similar properties. Rows are periods. Group 1 is the alkali metals, group 2 alkaline earth metals, group 17 halogens and group 18 noble gases.
Metals are on the left and center, are shiny, conduct electricity and tend to lose electrons. Nonmetals are on the upper right and tend to gain electrons. Metalloids lie along the staircase line.

Trends: atomic radius increases down a group and decreases across a period. Electronegativity and ionization energy increase across a period and decrease down a group. Fluorine is the most electronegative element.
units.try:
Rank Na, Mg and Cl by atomic radius, largest first.
Step 1: All are in period 3.
Step 2: Across a period, more protons pull electrons in tighter, so radius shrinks.
Step 3: Order: Na > Mg > Cl.
check: Elements in the same group share what?
The same number of valence electrons
Which group contains the unreactive noble gases?

learn: Atoms bond to reach a stable arrangement, usually eight valence electrons (the octet rule). Hydrogen and helium are stable with two.

Ionic bonds form when a metal transfers electrons to a nonmetal, making oppositely charged ions that attract, as in NaCl. Ionic compounds form crystals, have high melting points and conduct electricity when melted or dissolved.
Covalent bonds form when nonmetals share electrons, as in H₂O. Unequal sharing makes a polar bond. Metallic bonds are a sea of shared electrons among metal atoms.
Lewis dot structures show valence electrons. VSEPR theory predicts shape: CO₂ is linear, H₂O is bent, CH₄ is tetrahedral with 109.5° angles.
units.try:
Write the formula for the ionic compound of magnesium and chlorine.
Step 1: Mg loses 2 electrons → Mg²⁺. Cl gains 1 → Cl⁻.
Step 2: Charges must balance: one Mg²⁺ needs two Cl⁻.
Step 3: Formula: MgCl₂.
Now try aluminum and oxygen. (Answer: Al₂O₃.)
check: What kind of bond forms when electrons are shared?
What is the shape of a water molecule?

learn: Ionic compounds are named cation first, then anion with -ide: NaCl is sodium chloride. Transition metals use Roman numerals for charge: FeCl₃ is iron(III) chloride.
Polyatomic ions are groups that act as one ion, such as sulfate SO₄²⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻, hydroxide OH⁻ and ammonium NH₄⁺.
Covalent (molecular) compounds use prefixes: mono-, di-, tri-, tetra-, penta-. CO is carbon monoxide; N₂O₄ is dinitrogen tetroxide.
Common acids: HCl is hydrochloric acid, H₂SO₄ is sulfuric acid, HNO₃ is nitric acid.
units.try:
Name Ca(NO₃)₂ and write the formula for sodium sulfate.
Step 1: Ca²⁺ is calcium; NO₃⁻ is nitrate → calcium nitrate.
Step 2: Sodium is Na⁺; sulfate is SO₄²⁻.
Step 3: Two Na⁺ balance one SO₄²⁻ → Na₂SO₄.
check: What is the name of CO₂?
What is the formula of the hydroxide ion?

learn: A chemical equation shows reactants turning into products. The law of conservation of mass says atoms are not created or destroyed, so equations must be balanced using coefficients.
Never change subscripts to balance an equation; that would change the substance. Change only coefficients.
Reaction types: synthesis (A + B → AB), decomposition (AB → A + B), single replacement (A + BC → AC + B), double replacement (AB + CD → AD + CB) and combustion (fuel + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O).
Reaction rates increase with higher temperature, higher concentration, greater surface area and catalysts, which speed reactions without being used up.
units.try:
Balance: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O.
Step 1: Oxygen: 2 on left, 1 on right. Put 2 before H₂O: H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
Step 2: Hydrogen: now 4 on right, 2 on left. Put 2 before H₂: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
Step 3: Check: 4 H and 2 O on each side. Balanced.
check: What do you change to balance an equation?
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O is what type of reaction?

learn: A mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles, called Avogadro’s number. It lets chemists count atoms by weighing.
Molar mass is the mass of one mole in grams, found by adding atomic masses. Water, H₂O, has molar mass 2(1.01) + 16.00 = 18.02 g/mol.
Stoichiometry uses mole ratios from a balanced equation to predict amounts. In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 2 moles of H₂ make 2 moles of water.
The limiting reactant runs out first and determines how much product forms. Percent yield = (actual ÷ theoretical) × 100%.
units.try:
How many grams of water form from 4.0 g of H₂ with plenty of O₂? (2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O)
Step 1: Moles H₂ = 4.0 g ÷ 2.02 g/mol ≈ 1.98 mol.
Step 2: Ratio H₂ : H₂O is 2 : 2, so 1.98 mol H₂O.
Step 3: Mass = 1.98 × 18.02 ≈ 35.7 g of water.
check: How many particles are in one mole?
What is the molar mass of CO₂ (C = 12.01, O = 16.00)?

units.t: States of Matter and Gas Laws
learn: Kinetic molecular theory says particles are always moving. Temperature measures their average kinetic energy. Solids vibrate in place, liquids slide past each other, gases move freely.
Gas laws use kelvin: K = °C + 273. Boyle’s law: at constant temperature, P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. Charles’s law: at constant pressure, V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂.
The combined gas law is P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂. The ideal gas law is PV = nRT, where R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K).
At standard temperature and pressure (0 °C and 1 atm), one mole of an ideal gas occupies about 22.4 L.
units.try:
A balloon holds 2.0 L at 27 °C. What is its volume at 87 °C, same pressure?
Step 1: Convert: 27 + 273 = 300 K; 87 + 273 = 360 K.
Step 2: V₂ = V₁ × T₂/T₁ = 2.0 × 360/300.
Step 3: V₂ = 2.4 L.
check: If pressure on a gas doubles at constant temperature, its volume does what?

learn: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent. Water is called the universal solvent because its polar molecules dissolve many substances. The rule is “like dissolves like.”
Molarity M = moles of solute ÷ liters of solution. A 2 M solution has 2 moles per liter.
Solubility usually increases with temperature for solids but decreases for gases, which is why warm soda goes flat faster.
Dilution follows M₁V₁ = M₂V₂. Adding solute to water lowers the freezing point and raises the boiling point; these are colligative properties, which is why salt melts icy roads.
units.try:
How do you make 500 mL of 0.5 M NaCl from a 2.0 M stock?
Step 1: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ → 2.0 × V₁ = 0.5 × 500.
Step 2: V₁ = 250 ÷ 2.0 = 125 mL.
Step 3: Measure 125 mL of stock and add water to a total of 500 mL.
check: Moles of solute per liter of solution
Why does salt help melt ice on roads?
It lowers the freezing point of water

learn: Acids release H⁺ ions in water, taste sour and turn blue litmus red. Bases release OH⁻ ions, taste bitter, feel slippery and turn red litmus blue. Never taste lab chemicals.
The pH scale runs from 0 to 14. pH 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic, above 7 is basic. Each step is a factor of 10: pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4. pH = −log[H⁺].
Neutralization: acid + base → salt + water, as in HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.
Reactions that release heat are exothermic (burning); those that absorb heat are endothermic (an instant cold pack). Activation energy is the energy needed to start a reaction.
units.try:
A solution has [H⁺] = 1 × 10⁻⁴ M. Find its pH and classify it.
Step 1: pH = −log(1 × 10⁻⁴).
Step 2: pH = 4.
Step 3: Since 4 < 7, it is acidic.
How much more acidic is it than a pH 6 solution? (Answer: 100 times.)
check: A solution with pH 10 is what?
What does an acid and a base react to form?

rooms.about: A survey of United States history from Reconstruction to the present, covering industrialization, reform, two world wars, the Cold War, civil rights and modern America.

learn: After the Civil War ended in 1865, Reconstruction (1865–1877) tried to rebuild the South and define freedom for about 4 million formerly enslaved people. The 13th Amendment (1865) abolished slavery, the 14th (1868) guaranteed citizenship and equal protection, and the 15th (1870) barred denying the vote because of race.
The Freedmen’s Bureau built schools and helped families reunite. Black men voted and were elected to office, including Hiram Revels, the first Black U.S. senator.
Many white Southerners resisted with Black Codes and violence by groups such as the Ku Klux Klan. Sharecropping trapped many families in debt.

Reconstruction ended with the Compromise of 1877, when federal troops left the South. Jim Crow laws then enforced segregation, and poll taxes and literacy tests took away Black voting rights for decades.
units.try: Make a timeline of the three Reconstruction Amendments with the year and one sentence on what each did. Then write a paragraph explaining why rights written into law were not fully protected in practice after 1877.
check: What did the Compromise of 1877 lead to?
The start of the Civil War

learn: Between about 1870 and 1900, the US became an industrial power. Railroads (the first transcontinental line was finished in 1869), steel, oil and electricity transformed the economy. Business leaders built huge corporations and trusts.

Workers often faced long hours, low pay and dangerous conditions, including child labor. Unions such as the American Federation of Labor formed, and strikes like the 1894 Pullman Strike sometimes turned violent.

Millions of immigrants arrived, many through Ellis Island after 1892, from southern and eastern Europe, while Chinese immigrants faced the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882. Cities grew quickly, with crowded tenements.

In the West, settlers, railroads and the US Army pushed Native nations onto reservations. Conflicts such as the Wounded Knee Massacre in 1890 and the near destruction of the buffalo devastated Plains peoples.
units.try: Imagine you are a 14-year-old factory worker in 1890. Write a journal entry of about 150 words describing your day, using at least three accurate details about working conditions from this unit.
check: What did the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 do?
What was a major goal of labor unions?

learn: Progressives (about 1890–1920) worked to fix problems of industrial society. Journalists called muckrakers exposed abuses; Upton Sinclair’s The Jungle (1906) led to the Meat Inspection Act and Pure Food and Drug Act.

Reforms included antitrust laws, the 16th Amendment (federal income tax), the 17th (direct election of senators) and the 19th (1920), which gave women the right to vote after decades of suffrage activism.
Progress was uneven. Many reforms ignored or excluded Black Americans; leaders like Ida B. Wells campaigned against lynching and W.E.B. Du Bois helped found the NAACP in 1909.
The US also expanded abroad. After the Spanish-American War of 1898 it gained Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, and it annexed Hawaii. Americans debated whether empire fit the nation’s ideals.
units.try: Choose one Progressive reform. Write a short report answering: What problem did it address? Who pushed for it? What changed? Who was left out?
check: Which amendment gave women the right to vote?
Journalists who exposed corruption and abuses

learn: World War I began in Europe in 1914. The US stayed neutral until 1917, when German submarine attacks and the Zimmermann Telegram pushed it to join. About 116,000 Americans died.
President Wilson proposed the Fourteen Points and a League of Nations, but the Senate refused to join the League.

The 1920s brought cars, radio, jazz and a booming stock market. The Harlem Renaissance celebrated Black writers and artists such as Langston Hughes and Zora Neale Hurston. The Great Migration moved Black families from the South to Northern cities.
The decade also saw tension: Prohibition of alcohol (1920–1933) led to organized crime, immigration was sharply limited in 1924, and the Klan grew again.
units.try: Make a two-column list titled “Roaring Twenties” and “Troubled Twenties.” Add four facts to each. Then write two sentences on whether the label “Roaring Twenties” is fair.
check: A flowering of Black art, music and writing
Which country did the US Senate refuse to let the nation join?

units.t: The Great Depression and New Deal
learn: The stock market crashed in October 1929. By 1933 about 25% of workers were unemployed, thousands of banks had failed, and farm families on the Great Plains suffered through the Dust Bowl.
President Franklin D. Roosevelt, elected in 1932, launched the New Deal: relief for the needy, recovery for the economy and reform to prevent another crash.
Programs included the Civilian Conservation Corps and Works Progress Administration (jobs), the FDIC (insuring bank deposits) and Social Security (1935) for retirees.
Critics said the New Deal went too far or not far enough. It greatly expanded the federal government’s role, and full recovery came with World War II spending.
units.try: Find out whether your area has a park, bridge or building built by the CCC or WPA (many towns do). Write three sentences about it, or describe one New Deal program that still exists and how it affects people today.
check: About what percent of workers were unemployed in 1933?
Which New Deal program still provides retirement income?

learn: World War II began in Europe in 1939. The US entered after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941. Americans fought in Europe, North Africa and the Pacific.

On the home front, women took factory jobs, families rationed goods, and the economy surged. About 120,000 Japanese Americans, most of them citizens, were forced into incarceration camps, a wrong the government formally apologized for in 1988.
The Holocaust was the Nazi regime’s systematic murder of six million Jews and millions of others. Allied troops liberated camps in 1945.
The war in Europe ended in May 1945. In August the US dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and Japan surrendered. More than 400,000 Americans died, and about 70 million people worldwide.
units.try: Interview an older relative or neighbor about what they know of their family’s experience in the 1940s, or read a firsthand account from your library. Write down three things you learned and one question you still have.
check: What event brought the US into World War II?
What happened to about 120,000 Japanese Americans during the war?
They were forced into incarceration camps
They were drafted into the navy

learn: After 1945 the US and Soviet Union became rivals in a Cold War between capitalist democracy and communism. The US followed containment, trying to stop communism from spreading.

Key events: the Marshall Plan rebuilt Western Europe, NATO formed in 1949, the Korean War (1950–1953), the space race after Sputnik in 1957, and the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962, when nuclear war seemed close.
At home, fear of communism led to the Red Scare and McCarthyism, when people were accused with little evidence.
The Vietnam War divided Americans; more than 58,000 Americans and millions of Vietnamese died. The Cold War ended when the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.
units.try: Draw a simple world map sketch and mark five Cold War hot spots from this unit with the year. Next to each, write one sentence on what happened.
check: What was the US policy of containment?
Building a wall around the US
In what year did the Soviet Union collapse?

learn: In Brown v. Board of Education (1954), the Supreme Court ruled school segregation unconstitutional. The Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–1956), sparked by Rosa Parks, brought Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. to national leadership.
Activists used nonviolent protest: sit-ins, Freedom Rides, the 1963 March on Washington and the Selma marches. Many faced arrests, beatings and murder.
The Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned discrimination in public places and employment. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 ended literacy tests and protected Black voters.
Other groups organized too: Mexican American farmworkers with César Chávez and Dolores Huerta, the women’s movement, and Native American and disability rights activists.
units.try: Read a short excerpt from a civil rights speech or letter in your library. Identify one example of ethos, pathos and logos, and explain in a paragraph how the speaker tried to persuade the nation.
check: What did Brown v. Board of Education decide?
What did the Voting Rights Act of 1965 do?
Ended literacy tests and protected voters

learn: The Watergate scandal led President Nixon to resign in 1974, the only president to do so. The 1970s also brought high inflation and an energy crisis.

The environmental movement led to the first Earth Day in 1970 and the Environmental Protection Agency. Title IX (1972) banned sex discrimination in schools receiving federal money, expanding girls’ sports.
In the 1980s, President Reagan cut taxes and expanded defense spending. The personal computer and later the internet began changing work and daily life.
The 1990s saw a strong economy, the end of the Cold War, the Americans with Disabilities Act (1990), and growing debates about immigration and the role of government.
units.try: Pick one law from this unit (EPA, Title IX or ADA). Find one place in your school or town where you can see its effects, and write a short paragraph describing it.
check: Bans sex discrimination in schools receiving federal funds

units.t: The United States in the 21st Century
learn: On September 11, 2001, terrorists attacked the US, killing nearly 3,000 people. The US went to war in Afghanistan and later Iraq, and created the Department of Homeland Security.
The 2008 financial crisis caused a deep recession. In 2009, Barack Obama became the first Black president.
Technology, especially smartphones and social media, reshaped communication, news and politics. Debates continued over health care, immigration, climate and the economy.
The COVID-19 pandemic beginning in 2020 disrupted schools, jobs and health worldwide. Historians remind us that recent events are still being studied, and people hold many viewpoints about them.
units.try: Choose one recent event. Find two news sources with different perspectives on it. List the facts both agree on and one point where they differ, then explain how a historian might check which claims are accurate.
check: Who became the first Black US president in 2009?

rooms.about: Intermediate Spanish: review of past tenses, the future and conditional, an introduction to the subjunctive, commands and pronouns, with readings and culture from across the Spanish-speaking world.

units.t: Repaso: el presente y la identidad
learn: We start by reviewing the present tense. Regular verbs follow patterns: hablar → hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan. Comer → como, comes, come. Vivir → vivo, vives, vive.
Stem-changing verbs change in all forms except nosotros and vosotros: querer → quiero (e→ie), poder → puedo (o→ue), pedir → pido (e→i).
Ser describes identity, origin and traits (Soy de Texas, Es simpática). Estar describes location and conditions (Estoy cansado, La biblioteca está cerca).
Talking about yourself: ¿Cómo eres? Soy trabajador y un poco tímido. ¿Qué te gusta hacer? Me gusta leer y jugar al fútbol.
units.try: Write six sentences in Spanish introducing yourself: name, origin (ser), personality (ser), how you feel today (estar), where you are (estar), and two activities you like (me gusta + infinitive). Read them aloud.
check: Which verb do you use in “The library is near”?

learn: Spanish has two simple past tenses. The preterite (pretérito) tells completed actions at a specific time: Ayer comí tacos. Regular endings: -é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -aron for -ar verbs; -í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -ieron for -er and -ir.

The imperfect (imperfecto) describes ongoing or habitual past actions, background, age, time and feelings: Cuando era niño, jugaba en el parque. Endings: -aba, -abas, -aba for -ar; -ía, -ías, -ía for -er/-ir. Only three verbs are irregular: ser (era), ir (iba), ver (veía).
Clue words help: ayer, una vez, el año pasado often go with the preterite; siempre, todos los días, mientras often go with the imperfect.
Together they tell stories: Llovía (background) cuando mi hermano llegó (interrupting action).
units.try: Write a five-sentence story about a childhood memory. Use the imperfect for at least two background details (weather, age, feelings) and the preterite for at least three events. Underline each verb and label it P or I.
check: Which tense fits “When I was young, I used to swim”?
What is the preterite yo form of comer?

learn: Many common verbs have irregular preterite stems with endings -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron (no accent marks): tener → tuve, estar → estuve, poder → pude, poner → puse, hacer → hice (él hizo), querer → quise, venir → vine.
Verbs with j-stems use -eron in the ellos form: decir → dije, dijeron; traer → traje, trajeron.
Ser and ir share the same preterite forms: fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fueron. Context tells you which verb is meant.
Family vocabulary: los abuelos, los tíos, los primos, el sobrino, la nieta, el padrastro, la madrastra, los suegros (in-laws).
units.try: Describe a family celebration from last year in six sentences using irregular preterites: ¿Quién vino? ¿Qué hicieron? ¿Qué trajeron? Example: Mis tíos vinieron y trajeron pastel.
check: What is the preterite yo form of tener?

learn: The simple future adds endings to the whole infinitive: -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án. Hablaré = I will speak. Comerás = you will eat.
The conditional uses the same stems with -ía endings: hablaría (I would speak), viviríamos (we would live). It expresses polite requests and hypotheticals: ¿Podrías ayudarme?
Irregular stems are shared by both: tener → tendr-, salir → saldr-, poner → pondr-, venir → vendr-, hacer → har-, decir → dir-, poder → podr-, saber → sabr-, querer → querr-.
Spanish also uses ir + a + infinitive for the near future: Voy a estudiar esta noche.
units.try: Write five predictions about your life in 2040 using the future tense (Viviré en..., Tendré...). Then write three sentences about what you would do with a free year using the conditional (Viajaría a...).
check: What is “we will have” in Spanish?
I will do the homework tomorrow

learn: Informal affirmative tú commands use the él form of the present: ¡Habla! ¡Come! Eight are irregular: di, haz, ve, pon, sal, sé, ten, ven.
Negative tú commands and all formal (usted/ustedes) commands use subjunctive forms: No hables. No comas. Hable usted. Coman ustedes.
Direct object pronouns (lo, la, los, las) replace the thing acted on; indirect object pronouns (me, te, le, nos, les) show to whom. Le and les become se before lo or la: Se lo doy.
Pronouns attach to affirmative commands (Dámelo) but go before negative ones (No me lo des). Adding pronouns may require an accent to keep the stress.
units.try: Write a recipe for a simple sandwich in five tú commands, then rewrite it in usted commands. Add one sentence with a double object pronoun, such as Pásamelo.
check: What is the affirmative tú command of poner?
How do you say “Don’t eat it (la manzana)” to a friend?

learn: The subjunctive is a mood used for wishes, doubts, emotions and recommendations about another person’s actions. Form it from the yo present, drop -o, and add opposite endings: hablar → hable; comer → coma; tener → tenga.
WEIRDO is a handy memory aid: Wishes, Emotions, Impersonal expressions, Recommendations, Doubt/denial, Ojalá. Example: Quiero que tú vengas. Es importante que estudiemos.
The subjunctive usually appears after que when the subject changes. Same subject uses the infinitive: Quiero ir (I want to go) but Quiero que vayas (I want you to go).
Irregulars: ser → sea, ir → vaya, saber → sepa, estar → esté, dar → dé, haber → haya.
units.try: Write six sentences giving advice to a new student, each using a different trigger: Te recomiendo que..., Es necesario que..., Ojalá que..., Espero que..., Dudo que..., Me alegra que...
check: Which sentence correctly uses the subjunctive?
Espero que tengas un buen día
Espero que tienes un buen día
Espero tener que tú un día
What is the subjunctive yo/él form of ir?

learn: Body vocabulary: la cabeza, el cuello, la espalda, el estómago, el brazo, la mano, la rodilla, el pie, los dedos, la garganta.
To describe pain, use doler like gustar: Me duele la cabeza. Me duelen los pies. Other expressions: tengo fiebre, tengo tos, estoy resfriado, me torcí el tobillo.
At the doctor’s office: el médico, la enfermera, la receta (prescription), las pastillas, el jarabe (syrup), la cita (appointment), la sala de emergencia.
Many Spanish-speaking countries have public health systems and neighborhood farmacias where pharmacists give basic advice.
units.try: Write a short dialogue of eight lines between a patient and a doctor. The patient describes two symptoms with doler and tener; the doctor gives two recommendations using the subjunctive (Le recomiendo que descanse).
check: How do you say “My feet hurt”?
What is una receta at the doctor’s?

learn: Environment vocabulary: el medio ambiente, la contaminación, reciclar, la basura, la selva tropical, la sequía (drought), el calentamiento global, la energía solar, proteger, conservar.
Latin America holds great biodiversity: the Amazon rainforest spreads across nine countries, and Costa Rica protects about a quarter of its land in parks and reserves.
Use impersonal expressions with the subjunctive to discuss solutions: Es necesario que reciclemos. Es urgente que conservemos el agua.
Use se for general statements: Se debe apagar la luz. Se prohíbe tirar basura.
units.try: Create a poster in Spanish for your school with a title and five suggestions to protect the environment, using at least three es + adjective + que + subjunctive phrases.
check: Complete: Es importante que nosotros ___ el agua.

units.t: El arte y la literatura hispana
learn: Diego Rivera painted giant murals in Mexico showing workers and history. Frida Kahlo painted vivid self-portraits about pain and identity. Pablo Picasso of Spain co-founded Cubism.

Literature: Miguel de Cervantes wrote Don Quijote (1605), often called the first modern novel. Pablo Neruda of Chile and Gabriela Mistral, the first Latin American Nobel Prize winner in literature (1945), were celebrated poets.
To describe art: el cuadro, el retrato, el paisaje, el mural, los colores vivos, en primer plano (in the foreground), al fondo (in the background).
Opinions: Me parece que..., En mi opinión..., Lo que más me gusta es...
units.try: Find an image of a painting by a Spanish or Latin American artist in a library book. Describe it in Spanish in six sentences: what is in the foreground and background, the colors, and your opinion.
check: What does al fondo mean when describing a painting?

learn: Travel vocabulary: el pasaporte, el equipaje, la maleta, el vuelo, la aduana (customs), facturar (check bags), el andén (platform), la reserva, el alojamiento.
Asking for directions: ¿Cómo llego a...? Siga derecho. Doble a la izquierda. Está a dos cuadras.

Por and para both mean “for” but differ. Para shows purpose, destination and deadlines (para Lima, para el lunes). Por shows cause, exchange, duration and route (por dos horas, por el parque, gracias por todo).
Planning a trip combines tenses: future (Visitaré Perú), conditional (Me gustaría ver Machu Picchu) and subjunctive (Ojalá que haga buen tiempo).
units.try: Plan a three-day trip to a Spanish-speaking city. Write an itinerary in Spanish with at least eight sentences using the future, the conditional, one Ojalá que with subjunctive, and correct uses of por and para.
check: Which is correct: “I left for Lima”?

rooms.about: Building on Visual Art I, students deepen drawing, painting, printmaking, sculpture and design skills, study art history, and begin developing a personal voice through critique.

learn: Strong art begins with careful looking. Contour drawing traces edges; blind contour drawing keeps your eyes on the subject, not the paper, to train hand-eye coordination.
Sighting uses a pencil held at arm’s length to measure proportions and angles. Compare everything to one unit, such as the height of a head.
Value is lightness or darkness. A full value scale runs from white to black in steps. Light on a form shows highlight, mid-tone, core shadow, reflected light and cast shadow.
Hatching, cross-hatching, stippling and blending are ways to build value.
units.try: Set a white mug or egg near a lamp. Spend 20 minutes drawing it, using sighting for proportions and shading all five parts of light: highlight, mid-tone, core shadow, reflected light and cast shadow.
check: Drawing edges while looking only at the subject
Drawing with eyes closed and no subject
Which part of light appears on the table beside an object?

learn: Linear perspective creates depth on a flat surface. It was developed in Renaissance Florence, often credited to the architect Filippo Brunelleschi around 1415.
The horizon line is at the viewer’s eye level. Parallel lines going away from you meet at a vanishing point on the horizon.

One-point perspective has one vanishing point, good for roads and hallways. Two-point perspective has two, good for buildings seen from a corner. Three-point adds a point above or below for dramatic views.
Atmospheric perspective adds depth by making distant objects lighter, bluer and less detailed.
units.try: Draw a street in two-point perspective. Use a ruler to set a horizon line and two vanishing points near the paper edges. Draw at least three boxy buildings with windows and doors, all lines guided to the correct points.
check: At the bottom of the page
Making distant things lighter and less detailed

learn: The color wheel has primary colors (red, yellow, blue), secondary colors (orange, green, violet) and tertiary colors mixed from a primary and a neighboring secondary.
Hue is the color name. Value is lightness: add white for a tint, black for a shade. Intensity or saturation is brightness: mixing a color with its complement lowers it.
Color schemes: complementary (opposites), analogous (neighbors), monochromatic (one hue in many values), triadic (three evenly spaced).
Warm colors seem to advance; cool colors seem to recede. Artists use temperature to suggest space and mood.
units.try: With any paints you have, make a 9-square chart: one hue, then three tints, three shades, and two squares where you mix in small amounts of its complement. Label each square.
check: A color mixed with its complement
Which colors form a complementary pair?

learn: Watercolor is transparent; work light to dark and let white paper be your white. Techniques include wet-on-wet (soft blends) and wet-on-dry (crisp edges).
Acrylic paint dries fast and can be opaque. Artists build an underpainting, then layer colors. Impasto means thick, textured paint.
Glazing is a thin transparent layer over dry paint that changes color while keeping depth.
Clean brushes with water for acrylic and watercolor, and never pour paint down drains in large amounts; wipe excess on paper towels first.
units.try: Paint a simple landscape of sky, hills and a tree. Use wet-on-wet for the sky and wet-on-dry for the tree. Notice and write down the difference in edges.
check: In watercolor, how do you usually get white?

learn: Printmaking makes multiple images from one prepared surface. Each print in a set is called an impression, and artists number editions like 3/20.
Relief printing, such as linocut or woodcut, carves away areas that will stay white; the raised surface gets inked. The image prints in reverse.
Intaglio printing, such as etching, holds ink in grooves below the surface. Japanese ukiyo-e woodblock prints by artists like Hokusai influenced European painters in the 1800s.
Monoprinting creates one unique print by painting on a smooth surface and pressing paper onto it.
units.try: Make a foam or eraser stamp: draw a simple design, press lines into foam with a dull pencil (or have an adult cut an eraser), roll or brush on paint, and print it four times in a pattern. Remember the image will be reversed.
check: In relief printing, which parts print?
Only the edges of the paper
What does an edition number like 3/20 mean?

learn: Sculpture has height, width and depth. Additive sculpture builds up material (clay modeling, assemblage). Subtractive sculpture carves away (stone, wood). Constructed sculpture joins parts.
Relief sculpture projects from a flat background; sculpture in the round can be viewed from all sides.
Consider mass, space, balance and how light falls on form. Negative space, the empty space around and through a sculpture, matters as much as solid form.
When joining clay, use the score-and-slip method: scratch both surfaces, add slip (watery clay), and press together.
units.try: Using aluminum foil, build a small figure in an action pose. Then cover it with masking tape and add details. Turn it all around and adjust so it looks good from every angle.
check: Carving away wood or stone is which method?
How do you join two pieces of clay?

learn: The Renaissance (about 1400–1600) revived classical ideas. Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo and Raphael used perspective, anatomy and balanced composition.
Baroque art (1600s) used drama and strong light and dark contrast called chiaroscuro, as in Caravaggio and Rembrandt.
Romanticism (late 1700s–1800s) celebrated emotion and nature; Realism showed everyday working life.
Impressionism (1870s France) captured changing light with quick visible brushstrokes, painted outdoors. Claude Monet, Berthe Morisot and Pierre-Auguste Renoir are key figures.
units.try: Make a timeline poster of the four movements from this unit. For each, sketch a small thumbnail in that style, such as a dramatic lamp-lit face for Baroque or a quick outdoor scene for Impressionism.
check: Strong contrast of light and dark
Which movement focused on changing outdoor light?

learn: Modern art (about 1880–1970) broke rules. Cubism, led by Picasso and Braque, showed objects from several viewpoints at once. Surrealism painted dreamlike scenes.
Abstract Expressionism in New York after 1945 used gesture and large fields of color. Jackson Pollock dripped paint; Mark Rothko painted glowing color rectangles.
Pop Art used images from ads and comics. Contemporary art (since about 1970) includes installation, video, performance and digital art.
Contemporary artists often explore identity, environment and society, and artists from every continent now shape the global art world.
units.try: Create a small Cubist self-portrait: draw your face from the front and from the side, cut both drawings into geometric pieces, and reassemble them into one image on new paper.
check: Showed objects from several viewpoints at once
Which is a contemporary art form?

learn: Graphic design communicates with images and text. Principles include hierarchy (what is seen first), alignment, contrast, repetition and white space.
Typography is the art of arranging type. Serif fonts have small feet at stroke ends; sans-serif fonts do not. Limit a design to two typefaces for clarity.
A logo should be simple, memorable and work in black and white and at small sizes.
Designers sketch thumbnails, refine one idea, and test it with viewers.
units.try: Design a poster for an imaginary school event. Sketch three thumbnails first, then make the final version with a clear headline, date and location, using hierarchy and no more than two fonts.
check: The order in which viewers notice elements
Small strokes or feet at letter ends

learn: A formal critique follows four steps: describe (what you see), analyze (how elements and principles are used), interpret (what it means) and judge (how successful it is, with reasons).
Give feedback that is specific and kind: name a strength, ask a question, then offer one suggestion.
An artist statement is a short paragraph explaining what you made, how you made it and why. Use first person and clear language.
Keep your best work and sketches together. Reflection on growth helps you develop a personal style.
units.try: Choose your favorite artwork from this year. Write a 100-word artist statement answering what, how and why. Then show it to a family member and ask for one strength and one suggestion.
check: What is the first step of a formal critique?
What does an artist statement explain?
What you made, how and why

rooms.about: A journey through Western music history from medieval chant to today, plus jazz, blues and world traditions, learning how music changed and how to listen critically.

learn: Music history studies how music changed over time and why. Styles grew from technology, religion, politics and who paid musicians.
Describe music with its elements: melody (tune), harmony (chords), rhythm (pattern of durations), tempo (speed), dynamics (loudness), timbre (tone color), texture and form.
Texture can be monophonic (one melody alone), homophonic (melody with chords) or polyphonic (several independent melodies at once).
Western music history is usually divided into eras: Medieval, Renaissance, Baroque, Classical, Romantic, and the 20th and 21st centuries.
units.try: Listen to any song you like. Write one sentence each about its melody, rhythm, tempo, dynamics, timbre and texture. Then decide if the texture is monophonic, homophonic or polyphonic.

learn: Medieval music (about 500–1400) centered on the church. Gregorian chant is monophonic, sung in Latin, with flexible rhythm. Hildegard of Bingen, a 12th-century abbess, composed chants still sung today.
Over time, composers added voices, creating organum and then polyphony. Musical notation developed, so music could be written down and preserved.
The Renaissance (about 1400–1600) brought smooth polyphony, as in the masses of Josquin des Prez and Palestrina. The printing press spread sheet music.
Secular songs grew popular too, like the English and Italian madrigal, where words were often painted in the music, such as a rising line on the word heaven.
units.try: Sing or hum one steady note while a family member sings a simple tune over it. You have made a drone, an early step toward harmony. Then try a round like Row, Row, Row Your Boat to hear polyphony.
check: Music that imitates the meaning of the words
Painting a picture during a concert

learn: Baroque music (about 1600–1750) features steady driving rhythms, ornamentation and basso continuo, a bass line with chords played by harpsichord and cello.
Opera was born around 1600 in Italy, combining drama, singing and orchestra. Claudio Monteverdi was an early master.
Johann Sebastian Bach wrote fugues, cantatas and the Brandenburg Concertos. George Frideric Handel wrote the oratorio Messiah (1741). Antonio Vivaldi wrote The Four Seasons violin concertos.
A fugue introduces a short theme called the subject in one voice, then imitates it in others. Terraced dynamics shift suddenly between loud and soft.
units.try: Listen to a movement from Vivaldi’s Four Seasons (school or library recordings often include it). Write down which season you think it is and three musical details that suggest that season.
check: A bass line with chords supporting the music

learn: The Classical era (about 1750–1820) valued balance, clarity and elegant melodies. Phrases often come in matching pairs, like a question and answer.
Major forms include the symphony (usually four movements for orchestra), the string quartet, the concerto and the sonata. Sonata form has an exposition, development and recapitulation.
Joseph Haydn wrote over 100 symphonies. Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart composed more than 600 works before dying at 35. Ludwig van Beethoven bridged into the Romantic era.
The piano replaced the harpsichord because it could play soft and loud, giving gradual dynamics like crescendo and decrescendo.
units.try: Listen to the first movement of a Classical symphony. Raise a hand each time the main theme returns. Write down roughly when the exposition, development and recapitulation seem to happen.
check: What are the three main sections of sonata form?
Why did the piano replace the harpsichord?
It could play gradual soft and loud dynamics

learn: Beethoven (1770–1827) expanded the symphony’s size and emotion. He kept composing after becoming deaf; his Ninth Symphony includes a choir singing the Ode to Joy.
Romantic music (about 1820–1900) emphasized emotion, imagination, nature and national identity. Orchestras grew larger and harmonies richer.
Composers include Frédéric Chopin (piano), Franz Schubert (art songs), Clara Schumann (pianist and composer), Pyotr Tchaikovsky (ballets) and Giuseppe Verdi (operas).
Program music tells a story or paints a scene without words. Nationalism led composers like Antonín Dvořák and Edvard Grieg to use folk melodies from their homelands.
units.try: Pick a scene from nature, like a storm. Using any instrument, pots, or your voice, create a 30-second piece of program music that tells the scene, with a calm beginning, a loud middle and a quiet ending.
check: Instrumental music that tells a story or paints a scene
Music printed in a concert program
What did Beethoven continue doing after becoming deaf?

learn: The blues grew from African American work songs, spirituals and field hollers in the Deep South in the late 1800s. It often uses a 12-bar form and blue notes, slightly lowered pitches.
A typical 12-bar blues uses three chords, I, IV and V, and lyrics in an AAB pattern: a line, the same line repeated, then a response.
Jazz began in New Orleans in the early 1900s, blending blues, ragtime, brass bands and African and Caribbean rhythms. Swing rhythm and improvisation are central.
Louis Armstrong made the trumpet solo famous; Duke Ellington led a great orchestra; Bessie Smith was called the Empress of the Blues.
units.try: Write your own blues lyric in AAB form about something small, like losing your homework. Line A states it, line A repeats it, line B answers. Clap a steady beat and chant it in rhythm.
check: How many bars are in a standard blues form?

learn: The 1900s brought radical change. Claude Debussy’s Impressionism used blurry harmonies. Igor Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring (1913) shocked Paris with pounding rhythms.
Arnold Schoenberg created twelve-tone music, which treats all 12 pitches equally and avoids a home key. Minimalists such as Steve Reich and Philip Glass used repeating patterns that shift slowly.
American composers drew on homegrown sources: George Gershwin blended jazz and classical in Rhapsody in Blue (1924); Aaron Copland used folk tunes in Appalachian Spring.
Recording technology, radio and film turned music into a mass medium and gave composers new tools like electronic sounds.
units.try: Make a minimalist piece: clap a simple four-beat pattern and repeat it 16 times, changing just one beat every four times. Notice how small changes stand out when everything else repeats.

learn: Rock and roll emerged in the 1950s from rhythm and blues, country and gospel. Black artists such as Chuck Berry and Little Richard were key pioneers.
The 1960s brought Motown, soul, folk protest songs and the British Invasion. Music became tied to civil rights and social movements.
Hip-hop began in the Bronx, New York, in the 1970s, with DJs looping drum breaks and MCs rapping. It grew into a worldwide culture including dance and visual art.
Many genres, from country to electronic dance music, share roots in African American musical traditions such as call and response, syncopation and the blues.
units.try: Make a family music timeline: ask relatives what songs they loved at your age. Place each song by decade and write which genre it belongs to and one feature you hear in it.
check: Rock and roll grew mainly from which styles?
Rhythm and blues, country and gospel

learn: Music everywhere reflects its culture. Indian classical music uses ragas (melodic frameworks) and talas (rhythmic cycles), played on instruments like the sitar and tabla.
Indonesian gamelan ensembles use bronze gongs and metallophones in interlocking layered patterns.
West African drumming often uses polyrhythm, several rhythms at once, and call and response between leader and group. The kora is a 21-string harp-lute.
Latin American styles such as salsa, tango, son and samba mix African, European and Indigenous roots. The clave rhythm underlies much Afro-Cuban music.
units.try: Learn the 3-2 son clave by clapping: in a count of 1-and-2-and-3-and-4-and twice, clap on 1, the and of 2, and 4, then on 2 and 3 of the next measure. Repeat until it feels natural.
check: A melodic framework in Indian classical music
Several different rhythms played at once

learn: A concert review describes, analyzes and evaluates a performance. Include the performers, pieces, era or style, and specific musical details.
Use music vocabulary precisely: instead of “it sounded good,” write “the brass crescendo built tension before the quiet return of the theme.”
Support opinions with evidence from the music, and consider the historical context of the piece.
Copyright protects composers’ work. Credit composers and performers when you use or discuss their music.
units.try: Attend a school concert, community performance or watch a recorded one. Write a 200-word review naming two pieces, describing three specific musical moments with vocabulary from this course, and giving a supported opinion.
check: What makes a strong concert review?
Specific musical details and supported opinions
Only saying whether you liked it
Which is the most precise description?
The strings swelled in a crescendo

rooms.about: A year of building fitness and making informed health decisions: training principles, nutrition, sleep, mental health, substance-use risks, healthy relationships, safety and first aid.

units.t: Components of Fitness and Goal Setting
learn: Health-related fitness has five components: cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition.
Skill-related fitness includes agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time and speed. These help in sports but matter less for overall health.
SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. “Get fit” is vague; “Jog 20 minutes without stopping, three times a week, by March 1” is SMART.
Track progress with simple tests: a timed mile or step test, push-ups, curl-ups and sit-and-reach. Compare yourself to your own past results, not to others.
units.try: Do a safe personal baseline: count push-ups (knees allowed) in 60 seconds, count curl-ups in 60 seconds, and time a comfortable 10-minute walk-jog distance. Write one SMART goal based on your results.
check: Which is a health-related fitness component?
Walk 30 minutes, 5 days a week, for 6 weeks

learn: The FITT principle adjusts exercise: Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard), Time (how long) and Type (what activity).
Overload means gradually doing more than your body is used to; progression means increasing slowly, about 10% a week. Specificity means you improve in what you train.
Teens should get at least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity daily, with muscle- and bone-strengthening activity at least 3 days a week.
Warm up for 5–10 minutes before exercise and cool down after. Stop if you feel sharp pain, dizziness or chest pain, and tell an adult.
units.try: Find your target heart rate zone: estimate max heart rate as 220 − age. For age 15, that is 205. Moderate to vigorous training is about 64–90% of max: 0.64 × 205 ≈ 131 to 0.90 × 205 ≈ 185 beats per minute. Walk briskly for 5 minutes, then count your pulse for 15 seconds and multiply by 4.
check: What does the I in FITT stand for?
How much daily activity is recommended for teens?

learn: The three macronutrients provide energy: carbohydrates (4 calories per gram), protein (4 per gram) and fat (9 per gram). Carbohydrates are the main fuel for exercise.
Fiber, vitamins, minerals and water are also essential. Teens need calcium and vitamin D for growing bones and iron for healthy blood.
Read nutrition labels: check serving size first, then calories, added sugars, sodium and fiber. The % Daily Value tells you if a nutrient is low (5% or less) or high (20% or more).
Hydrate before, during and after activity. Plain water works for most exercise under an hour.
units.try: Read the nutrition label on two snacks at home. Record serving size, calories, added sugars and fiber for each. Decide which is the better everyday choice and explain why in two sentences.
check: How many calories are in one gram of fat?
On a label, a % Daily Value of 20% or more means the nutrient is what?

learn: Teens need 8–10 hours of sleep a night. Sleep supports memory, mood, immune health, growth and athletic performance.
Good sleep habits: keep a regular schedule, keep screens out of bed for the last hour, limit caffeine after noon, and keep your room cool and dark.
Stress is the body’s response to challenges. Short-term stress can help you focus, but long-term stress can affect sleep, health and mood.
Healthy coping strategies include exercise, breaking big tasks into steps, deep breathing, time outdoors and talking with someone you trust.
units.try: Practice box breathing: breathe in for 4 counts, hold for 4, breathe out for 4, hold for 4. Repeat 4 times. Then keep a sleep log for one week, noting bedtime, wake time and how rested you feel.
check: How many hours of sleep do teens need?
Which is a healthy way to cope with stress?
Exercise or talking with someone you trust

learn: Mental health includes how we think, feel and act. Everyone has ups and downs, but feelings that last two weeks or more and interfere with daily life may signal a condition such as depression or anxiety.
Mental health conditions are common and treatable. About one in five teens experiences one, and talking about it reduces stigma.
Warning signs in yourself or a friend include withdrawal, big changes in sleep or eating, hopelessness or talk of self-harm. Take these seriously and tell a trusted adult right away.
Help is available from parents, school counselors, nurses, doctors and crisis lines. In the US, you can call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline any time.
units.try: Make a personal support card: write the names of three trusted adults, your school counselor’s name and office, and the number 988. Keep it in your wallet or phone case.
check: What should you do if a friend talks about self-harm?
Tell a trusted adult right away
What number reaches the US Suicide and Crisis Lifeline?

learn: The teen brain keeps developing until about age 25, especially the prefrontal cortex that handles decisions. Alcohol, nicotine and other drugs can interfere with this development and make addiction more likely.
Nicotine in cigarettes and vapes is highly addictive. Vaping aerosol can contain harmful chemicals and heavy metals.
Alcohol slows reaction time and judgment, and is involved in many teen injuries and car crashes. Misusing prescription drugs, including taking someone else’s pills, is dangerous and illegal.
Refusal skills help: say no clearly, give a reason, suggest something else, or leave. Most teens do not use these substances, even if it can seem otherwise.
units.try: Write and practice aloud three different ways to refuse an offer of a vape, such as “No thanks, I have practice,” “Not my thing,” or suggesting another activity. Practice with a family member.
check: Until about what age does the brain keep developing?
Say no clearly and suggest another activity

learn: Healthy relationships, whether friendships, family or dating, are built on respect, trust, honesty, good communication and equality.
Warning signs of unhealthy relationships include controlling behavior, checking someone’s phone, jealousy, insults, isolation from friends and any threats or violence.
Consent means freely agreeing to something. It must be clear, given without pressure and can be changed at any time. Respecting a no is always required, online and in person.
If you or a friend feels unsafe in a relationship, talk to a trusted adult or counselor. Help is available and it is never the victim’s fault.
units.try: Practice I-statements, a respectful way to share feelings: “I feel [emotion] when [situation] because [reason]. I would like [request].” Write three examples for common situations with friends or family.
check: Which is a sign of an unhealthy relationship?
Checking a partner’s phone without permission
Which statement about consent is true?
It can be changed at any time

learn: Communicable diseases spread from person to person through germs such as viruses and bacteria. Handwashing for 20 seconds, vaccines and staying home when sick prevent spread.
Vaccines train the immune system to recognize germs without causing the full illness. Antibiotics treat bacterial infections but do not work on viruses like colds and flu.
Noncommunicable diseases, such as heart disease, type 2 diabetes and many cancers, are linked to genetics and lifestyle. Physical activity, healthy eating, not smoking and sun protection lower risk.
Regular checkups, dental visits and knowing your family health history help catch problems early.
units.try: Make a personal prevention checklist with eight habits from this unit, such as wearing sunscreen of SPF 30 or more. Check off what you did each day for one week.
check: Do antibiotics treat viral infections like the common cold?
Which lowers the risk of heart disease?

learn: Team sports such as volleyball, basketball and soccer build cooperation, communication and strategy. Individual sports like tennis, swimming and running can be enjoyed for a lifetime.
Sportsmanship means following rules, respecting opponents and officials, and winning or losing with grace.
Skill learning has stages: cognitive (thinking through each step), associative (practicing and refining) and autonomous (the skill becomes automatic).
Prevent injuries with proper equipment, warm-ups, good technique, hydration and rest days. Use RICE for minor sprains: rest, ice, compression, elevation.
units.try: Pick one sport skill, such as a volleyball pass against a wall. Practice 50 repetitions over a week. Each day, rate your consistency from 1 to 5 and note which learning stage you think you are in.
check: In which stage of skill learning is the skill automatic?
What does the C in RICE stand for?

learn: In an emergency, check the scene for safety, call 911 (or have someone call), and care for the person until help arrives.
For severe bleeding, apply firm direct pressure with a clean cloth. For a minor burn, cool it under cool running water for about 10 minutes.

Hands-only CPR for an adult who collapses and is not breathing normally: call 911, then push hard and fast in the center of the chest, at least 2 inches deep, 100–120 times a minute. Use an AED as soon as one arrives.
Prevent injuries: wear seat belts every ride, never text while driving, wear helmets for biking and skating, and learn to swim.
units.try: Practice the rhythm of hands-only CPR on a firm pillow: push to the beat of a song around 100–120 beats per minute, such as one with a steady disco beat, for 30 seconds. Then find where the nearest AED is in your school.
check: What is the correct rate for chest compressions?
How should you treat a minor burn?
Cool it under cool running water

rooms.about: A first full course in Python: variables, input and output, decisions, loops, functions, lists, dictionaries, strings, files, and debugging, ending with a small project.
